newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD warms up to single European currency.
newsitem.headline: German SPD warms up to single European currency.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), hurt at the polls when they flirted with Euro-scepticism, now say the European Union's planned common currency is the best response to a dominant U.S. dollar.

SPD European affairs spokeswoman Heide Wieczorek-Zeul told parliament on Thursday the planned single currency could help save jobs and shield Europe from the harmful effects of fluctuations in the American economy.

Her statement, in a debate over current EU negotiations to reform the Maastricht treaty, stood in sharp contrast to the SPD's failed bid early this year to win votes in a state poll with calls to delay the economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The dollar needs a counter-weight," she said, arguing that shifts in the dollar's value had led to job losses in Europe.
"U.S. governments have been able up to now to unload their economic problems abroad and spread the burden of their economic fluctuations on to other shoulders through their monetary policy."

Bonn's main opposition party has been rethinking its EMU stand since falling on its face earlier this year with a Euro-sceptical campaign that even many Social Democrats said smacked of a right-wing "D-mark nationalism".
Voters in Baden-Wuerttemberg, where the SPD tried to tap grass-roots fears about losing the deutschemark, drummed the party out of the coalition government there in a March poll.

Analysts said that defeat helped convince foreign exchange markets that Chancellor Helmut Kohl faced no real opposition to his staunchly pro-European policies and would march full steam ahead to launch the single currency on schedule in 1999.
Opinion polls show that at least two-thirds of Germans still oppose giving up the mark for what they fear will be a weaker Euro currency.
But just as many if not more trust Kohl to defend Germany's interests in the EU the best, and agree with him that European integration is more a political than an economic issue.
Wieczorek-Zeul said EMU could not succeed without a political union to ensure a system of checks and balances for decisions made at the European level.
"We won't progress if we leave the EMU up to the finance ministers and place our bets on the big single market," she said.
The SPD spokeswoman also called for the Maastricht review to include a common jobs policy in the EU treaty, saying this was crucial to assure the Union the support of its citizens.

Wieczorek-Zeul charged Bonn's market-oriented policies had helped foster a downward spiral in the EU, with countries competing to cut wages, social benefits and ecological standards to attract investment from other member states.
The SPD wanted a minimum company tax across the Union to prevent companies from playing one member country against another, she said.
